---
title: "Quiz: the DP principle"
---

Short questions to test your understanding. Try each on paper first, then open the answer. Paths go from the top row to the bottom row of a cost image, one row down per step and at most one column sideways; $M(i, j)$ is the cost of the cheapest path to pixel $(i, j)$.

---

**Q1.** State the principle of optimality for minimal paths in one sentence. Why does it let us keep only one number per pixel?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
What could you do if a part of the best path were not the best way to its end pixel?
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Every part of an optimal path is itself optimal: if the best path to the bottom passes through $p$, its part up to $p$ is the cheapest path to $p$ (otherwise we could swap in the cheaper part). So for continuing paths only the **cheapest** way to reach $p$ matters, and one number per pixel, $M(p)$, is enough.
:::

---

**Q2.** Three cells above pixel $(i, j)$ have $M = 12, 9, 15$, and $C(i, j) = 4$. What is $M(i, j)$, and where does its pointer point?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$M(i, j) = 4 + \min(12, 9, 15) = 13$; the pointer points to the middle cell (straight up), the one with 9.
:::

---

**Q3.** Why does the greedy path (cheapest first pixel, then always the cheapest pixel below) usually fail?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
It decides each step by looking only at the next pixel. A cheap step can lead into an expensive region that cannot be left in time, because a path moves at most one column per row. DP avoids this by not committing to any step before the whole table is filled: the path is chosen from the end.
:::

---

**Q4.** An image gets twice as many rows (same width). Roughly what happens to the number of paths, and to the work of DP?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Hint"}
About $m \cdot 3^{n-1}$ paths, about $3nm$ operations.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
The number of paths is roughly **squared** (divided by $m$): $3^{2n-1}$ instead of $3^{n-1}$, so astronomically more. The DP work only **doubles**: it grows linearly with the number of pixels.
:::

---

**Q5.** You need only the **cost** of the best path, not the path. How much memory does DP need? And if you need the path?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
For the cost, one row of $M$ is enough: each row is computed from the previous one only. For the path, you also need the pointers of **every** cell (or the whole table $M$), to backtrack from the end.
:::

---

**Q6.** In the two-label chain of the graph-cut day ($E = \sum_p D_p(L_p) + \lambda\,\#\{\text{label changes}\}$), what are the stages, the states and the cost of a step? What is the "path"?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
Stages: the pixels along the line. States: the two labels. Each pixel-and-label pays its data cost $D_p(\ell)$, and a step that changes the label pays $\lambda$. The "path" is the labelling: one label per pixel. The same table, with 2 columns instead of $m$.
:::

---

**Q7.** Why is one raster-order pass of the distance transform not enough, while one row-by-row pass is enough for monotone paths?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
A monotone path only ever comes **from above**, so when row $i$ is filled, everything it needs (row $i-1$) is final. For the distance transform, the shortest way to the nearest background pixel may come from below or from the right, which a top-to-bottom, left-to-right pass has not seen yet. Each pass is DP with a fixed order; neither order covers all paths.
:::

---

**Q8.** *(math)* Paths go from the top-left to the bottom-right cell with steps right, down, or diagonally right-down. Write the recursion for $M$, and say in which order the table can be filled.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Answer"}
$M(0, 0) = C(0, 0)$ and $M(i, j) = C(i, j) + \min\big(M(i-1, j),\ M(i, j-1),\ M(i-1, j-1)\big)$, with $M = \infty$ outside the grid. Row by row, left to right (or column by column): all three cells on the right-hand side come earlier. This is the table that aligns two signals (dynamic time warping).
:::
